title: Milo and the Missing Endings
markdown:
Willow Creek was usually as peaceful as a sleepy dandelion puff. Milo the mouse lived there, whiskers that wiggled, eyes like tiny polished acorns. He loved bedtime. He loved the cozy nook, and he especially loved the stories Mama read. Lately something was wrong.

Every night the last page of the story was gone. Poof. Vanished like a crumb in a hungry badger's pouch. The brave knight never quite saved the dragon. The clever fox never quite outsmarted the farmer. It left a hollow feeling, like a biscuit with no jam. A prickle ran through Milo's whiskers. He had once jumped nearly a whole foot when a ladybug landed on his nose. He was easily startled. Missing endings startled him more.

Then he started noticing Lantern. Lantern was a moth wizard. His wings shimmered with captured starlight. He lived in the tallest oldest tree, the Great Library Oak, where the town's books were kept. Lately he buzzed about looking bothered, his glow dimming like a fading candle. He dropped his glasses. He forgot his quill. Once he tried to polish a book with a dandelion puff.

One evening the moon painted silver streaks. Milo saw Lantern zip from the oak, carrying something that sparkled faintly, like a fallen star. Milo's whiskers twitched. His well-loved satchel bounced as he ran.

"Where are you going, Lantern?"

Lantern startled. Feelers drooped like sad twigs. "Oh, Milo. It's complicated. Very complicated. You wouldn't understand, little one." His voice was a dry rustle.

Milo followed anyway. Lantern flew straight to the Great Library Oak. The tree was enormous, branches like reaching arms. Inside: books floor to ceiling. Old paper. Faint magic. Milo's nose tingled. Dust motes danced.

The inside was not only shelves. It was a maze that changed. Books tumbled and shifted, whispering and giggling as they passed. The air hummed, rustling paper, small jokes. A ladder of stacked atlases led nowhere twice. Milo's heart went thump-thump-thump. A book about grumpy trolls mumbled nearby, pages flapping like an angry frown. He smelled glue and dust and a little honey from a cookbook that had wandered. He stayed. His satchel bumped a spine. The spine said ouch, politely, in gilt.

Lantern flitted ahead, dimmer than usual, still a beacon. He waited at corners so Milo's little legs could catch up. "We must fix this quickly," he whispered, raspy as crumpled paper. "Or the stories will be broken forever. A bedtime without a proper ending. A child's heart needs the full story. A tale with a missing end is like a cookie with no chocolate chips."

Milo's whiskers drooped. He knew that cookie.

They came to a clearing in the stacks. On a polished table of ancient trunk lay a jumble of torn paper. Moonlight pooled on it. Pieces of endings: brave knights, talking animals, the last words of lullabies.

Lantern sighed, wind through dry reeds. He picked up a fragment. "This is from The Little Bear Who Found His Honey. He never did get to eat it."

A tiny crinkled bookmark popped out from behind a fat volume of fairy tales. It had a grumpy face, scribbled eyebrows, a downturned mouth.

"Turn back, little mouse!" it squeaked, rusty hinge of a voice. "It's too hard! You're just a tiny thing. Go home and nibble cheese. This is wizard's work."

Milo's fur bristled. He looked at the sad torn pages. He looked at Lantern, more moth than wizard now. He could run home. He could curl up and pretend. Cheese. Safety. The whisper was tempting. His courage wavered like a candle in a draft.

Then he saw a piece of paper with a single sparkling tear, still wet with moonlight. The end of the story about the lost star that found its way home. He remembered the click of that ending, the warmth.

"No," Milo said, surprisingly firm. "I won't go back. These stories matter." He scurried to Lantern's side. "What can I do?"

Lantern's many eyes blinked. Surprise, then a flicker of hope. "You want to help?"

"Yes." Milo puffed his tiny chest.

Lantern reached into a woven pouch on his leg and drew a small vial of luminous dust. It pulsed like a tiny captured galaxy. "Starlight dust. It can mend anything. But using it uses up my own light. Each grain is a tiny piece of my magic."

He unscrewed the vial. Shimmering particles wove themselves into the torn page of the lost star. The tear vanished. A tiny twinkling star took its place. Lantern's wings flickered. Dimmer. A favourite shiny stone given away.

Milo pointed to the open window. Moonbeams poured in, a silvery waterfall. "We can use those! I'll gather them. I'll be your moonbeam collector!"

"You think you can?"

"I can try!"

He raced to the window. Tiny paws batted at the moonbeams, herding them like a determined shepherd, coaxing the silver until it pooled around the torn pages. One beam tried to slip back out; Milo sat on the sill a moment, a mouse-shaped stopper, then nudged it down to the table. Lantern sprinkled the remaining dust, mixing it with the collected light. Milo darted and gathered. Lantern wove and mended. Quiet urgency. A symphony of light that did not need a conductor's speech. Dust motes, which had been only dust, joined in as if they had been waiting for work.

Slowly the pages healed. Paper joined, a seam like a scar that knew its job. Ink came back, letter by letter, as if the stories had been holding their breath. The knight's ending, dragon not quite slain until the last line said so. The fox's clever escape, farmer scratching his head. The little bear ate his honey, sticky grin. The lost star shone in its rightful place in the story's sky, no tear left.

Dawn touched the clouds pink and orange. The last page was mended. Lantern's wings were dimmer than usual, a constellation after a long night, but his eyes held a quieter light.

Milo panted. The rustling books no longer made him jump. He looked at the mended star-page, still faintly warm.

"Lantern," he said, no longer only a squeak. "Will you teach me how to gather moonbeams? And how to protect the stories?"

Lantern smiled, faint starlight brightening for a moment. "Oh, Milo. I think we're going to be very good friends."

They left the grumpy bookmark on its shelf, still advising cheese. The maze, for now, stayed still. Somewhere in Willow Creek, Mama would turn a last page that was actually there. Milo's satchel smelled of paper and moonlight. He practised, on the way home, batting at a leftover beam until it sat on his paw like a tame crumb.
